guide.title: Habits and states
guide.rule: Use the present simple for regular actions and states.
guide.example: The library opens at eight.

guide.title: Actions and changes
guide.rule: Use the present continuous for current actions, temporary arrangements and developing situations.
guide.example: More students are joining the club this term.

guide.title: State or activity?
guide.rule: A verb may change meaning: think can describe an opinion or the activity of considering.
guide.example: I think it is useful. I am thinking about the proposal.

guide.title: Past sequence
guide.rule: The past simple presents completed events in a sequence.
guide.example: She opened the envelope and read the note.

guide.title: Background action
guide.rule: The past continuous shows an activity in progress around a past event.
guide.example: We were rehearsing when the lights went out.

guide.title: Former habits
guide.rule: Used to describes past habits and states. Would can describe repeated past actions when the past context is clear.
guide.example: We used to live near the river. Every Sunday we would visit the market.

title: Present perfect
sections: Test skills · General Training Writing · Task 1

guide.title: Connection to now
guide.rule: The present perfect connects a past event with an unfinished period or a present result. Use the past simple for a specified finished time.
guide.example: I have written two pages today. I wrote the introduction yesterday.

guide.title: Activity or result
guide.rule: The perfect continuous emphasises an ongoing activity or duration; the perfect simple can emphasise a result or a count.
guide.example: I have been revising all morning. I have revised three chapters.

guide.title: For and since
guide.rule: For gives a length of time; since gives its starting point.
guide.example: They have worked together for two years, since their first project.

guide.title: Earlier past
guide.rule: Use the past perfect to look back from a past point to an earlier event.
guide.example: When the guests arrived, we had prepared the room.

guide.title: Duration before a past point
guide.rule: Use had been + verb-ing to focus on an earlier activity and its duration.
guide.example: They had been waiting for an hour when the doors opened.

guide.title: Chronology
guide.rule: A past-simple sequence and a past-perfect reference can show different event orders.
guide.example: She arrived and he cooked. She arrived after he had cooked.

title: Future 1
sections: Test skills · General Training Reading · Part 2

guide.title: Plans and arrangements
guide.rule: Present continuous can describe a definite arrangement; going to can describe an intention or a prediction based on evidence.
guide.example: We are meeting at six. We are going to organise a workshop.

guide.title: Will
guide.rule: Will can make a prediction, an offer, a promise or an immediate decision.
guide.example: Your bag looks heavy. I will carry it.

guide.title: Academic predictions
guide.rule: Expressions such as be likely to and be predicted to mark a prediction. Future forms may overlap in meaning.
guide.example: The proposed scheme is likely to attract more visitors.

guide.title: Schedules and time clauses
guide.rule: Use the present simple for timetables and normally use a present form after when, until or as soon as in a future time clause.
guide.example: The train leaves at seven. I will call when I arrive.

guide.title: Progress and completion
guide.rule: Future continuous describes activity at a future point. Future perfect describes completion before a future point.
guide.example: At noon I will be writing. By three I will have finished.

guide.title: Duration and earlier intentions
guide.rule: Future perfect continuous measures duration up to a future point. Was going to can describe a past intention.
guide.example: By June I will have been studying here for a year. I was going to leave, but I stayed.

guide.title: Countability
guide.rule: Countable nouns can have a singular and plural. Many uncountable nouns, such as advice and furniture, normally have no plural.
guide.example: A chair, three chairs; some furniture.

guide.title: Quantities
guide.rule: Use number and fewer with countable plurals; use amount and less with uncountables. A few and a little are more positive than few and little.
guide.example: We have a few chairs but little space.

guide.title: Context changes meaning
guide.rule: Some nouns have countable and uncountable uses with different meanings.
guide.example: The window is made of glass. There are two glasses on the table.

guide.title: Articles and meaning
guide.rule: Use a/an for a nonspecific singular countable item and the for an identifiable item. General plural or uncountable references often have no article.
guide.example: I bought a notebook. The notebook is blue. Books can be useful.

guide.title: Sounds and possession
guide.rule: Choose a/an by sound. Possessive determiners replace articles; independent possessive pronouns can follow of.
guide.example: An hour; a university; a friend of mine.

guide.title: Groups and distance
guide.rule: This/these and that/those mark distance. Each/every take singular forms; both refers to two and neither excludes two.
guide.example: Each participant has a card. Both cards are valid.

guide.title: Either, neither and none
guide.rule: Bare either/neither + singular noun takes a singular verb. With either/neither of a plural noun phrase, singular or plural agreement can be valid. None of a plural group can also take singular or plural agreement.
guide.example: Neither room has a window. Neither of the rooms has/have a window.

guide.title: Replace repeated nouns
guide.rule: Use subject pronouns as subjects, object pronouns after verbs or prepositions, and possessive pronouns without a following noun.
guide.example: Mina called me. This bag is hers.

guide.title: Self and mutual actions
guide.rule: Reflexives can refer back to the subject or add emphasis. Each other describes a mutual action.
guide.example: They introduced themselves, then helped each other.

guide.title: It, there and substitutes
guide.rule: Introductory it can express weather, time or an evaluation. There introduces existence. One/ones can replace countable nouns.
guide.example: It is late. There is a spare chair. I prefer the blue one.

guide.title: Describing nouns
guide.rule: Adjectives can come before nouns or after linking verbs. Opinion usually comes before more factual description.
guide.example: A lovely small room; the room looks bright.

guide.title: Feelings and causes
guide.rule: An -ed adjective can describe a person’s feeling; an -ing adjective can describe its cause.
guide.example: The talk was interesting, so we were interested.

guide.title: Describing actions
guide.rule: Adverbs can modify verbs or adjectives. Fast and hard can be adverbs; hardly means almost not.
guide.example: She works hard. She hardly ever arrives late.

guide.title: Comparatives and superlatives
guide.rule: Comparatives compare items; superlatives place one item within a group. Some forms are irregular.
guide.example: This route is shorter. It is the shortest route in the survey.

guide.title: Degrees and quantities
guide.rule: Much or slightly can modify a comparison. Use fewer with countable plurals and less with uncountable quantities.
guide.example: There are far fewer cars and much less noise.

guide.title: Parallel comparisons
guide.rule: As ... as expresses equality. The more ... the more links changes. Multiples can compare quantities explicitly.
guide.example: The second room is twice as large as the first.

guide.title: Adding detail after a noun
guide.rule: A noun phrase can include a prepositional phrase after its main noun.
guide.example: The books on the upper shelf are new.

guide.title: Reduced clauses
guide.rule: An -ing clause can describe an active relationship; a past-participle clause can describe a passive one.
guide.example: Students waiting outside; notes written yesterday.

guide.title: To-infinitive clauses
guide.rule: A to-infinitive after a noun can describe a purpose, decision or opportunity.
guide.example: An opportunity to practise; a place to study.

guide.title: Ability
guide.rule: Can/could often express general ability. Managed to or was able to can describe a particular successful past action. Use be able to after will or have.
guide.example: She could swim as a child. She managed to unlock the door.

guide.title: Deduction and possibility
guide.rule: Must can express a strong positive deduction; cannot a strong negative one. May, might and could can all express possibility.
guide.example: The lights are on; someone might be inside.

guide.title: Time and caution
guide.rule: A modal + have + past participle refers to a possible past situation. Modals can qualify an academic claim.
guide.example: They may have misunderstood. The result might indicate a change.

title: Modals 2
sections: Test skills · General Training Reading · Part 2

guide.title: Obligation and prohibition
guide.rule: Must/have to/need to can express necessity. Must not expresses prohibition; not have to means absence of necessity.
guide.example: You must not enter. You do not have to stay.

guide.title: Time and necessity
guide.rule: Use had to for past necessity and will have to for future necessity. Need not have + participle explicitly describes an unnecessary action that happened.
guide.example: I need not have printed it; a copy was provided.

guide.title: Advice and formal language
guide.rule: Should and ought to can offer advice. Formal requirements can also use be required to.
guide.example: Visitors are required to sign in.

guide.title: Backshift and meaning
guide.rule: When reporting from a later viewpoint, tenses may move back. A backshift is not always required when the information remains true.
guide.example: “I am working.” She said she was working.

guide.title: Reporting patterns
guide.rule: Reporting verbs have different patterns: say something, tell someone, promise to do, suggest doing.
guide.example: He told us the time. She suggested waiting.

guide.title: Questions and reference
guide.rule: Reported questions use statement order. Time and place references depend on the reporting situation.
guide.example: He asked where I lived. “Tomorrow” may become “the following day”.

guide.title: Choosing a second verb
guide.rule: The first verb controls whether the next verb uses to, -ing or a bare infinitive. Some verbs allow more than one pattern.
guide.example: Decide to apply; enjoy learning; let someone leave.

guide.title: Meaning changes
guide.rule: Remember doing recalls an event; remember to do means not forgetting a task. Stop doing ends an action; stop to do interrupts another action for a purpose.
guide.example: I remembered posting it. I remembered to post it.

guide.title: Objects, passives and negatives
guide.rule: Make and let take an object and bare infinitive. Passive made takes to. A negative can be placed before the second verb.
guide.example: They made us wait. We were made to wait. I chose not to go.

guide.title: Facts and probable results
guide.rule: Zero conditionals describe regular connections. First conditionals describe an open future condition and result.
guide.example: If you press this fictional switch, the light comes on. If it rains, we will meet inside.

guide.title: Hypothetical situations
guide.rule: The second conditional imagines an unreal or unlikely present or future situation.
guide.example: If I had a larger desk, I would keep the model there.

guide.title: Other condition markers
guide.rule: Unless means if not. In case introduces a precaution. Provided that and as long as can set a condition.
guide.example: Take a copy in case the original is lost.

guide.title: An unreal past
guide.rule: The third conditional imagines a different past and its past result.
guide.example: If we had checked the address, we would have arrived on time.

guide.title: Mixed reference times
guide.rule: Mixed conditionals connect different times, such as an earlier action and a present result.
guide.example: If I had kept the receipt, I would have proof now.

guide.title: Wishes and regrets
guide.rule: Wish + past form can describe an unreal present; wish + past perfect expresses a past regret. Should have evaluates an earlier action.
guide.example: I wish I knew. I wish I had asked. I should have asked.

guide.title: Collocations
guide.rule: The preposition can be controlled by the verb, adjective or noun. Learn the whole phrase.
guide.example: Depend on; interested in; a reason for.

guide.title: Patterns and forms
guide.rule: After a preposition, a following verb normally uses -ing. Some verbs, such as marry, take a direct object.
guide.example: She apologised for arriving late. He married his partner.

guide.title: Prepositional phrases
guide.rule: Phrases can express manner, time, transport or circumstance.
guide.example: By email; on purpose; in the end; at first.

guide.title: Defining information
guide.rule: Defining relatives identify which person or thing is meant. An object relative pronoun can often be omitted.
guide.example: The book I borrowed is useful.

guide.title: Extra information
guide.rule: Non-defining relatives add extra information and use commas. They do not normally use that. Which can refer to a preceding idea.
guide.example: The talk, which lasted an hour, was useful.

guide.title: Possession and formal prepositions
guide.rule: Whose expresses possession. Formal preposition + whom/which can replace a preposition at the end.
guide.example: The tutor to whom I wrote; the room in which we met.

guide.title: Subjects and information flow
guide.rule: A noun phrase can foreground the topic. Introductory it can prepare for a longer subject. Known information often leads to new information.
guide.example: It is useful to compare both plans. Both plans contain a shared workspace.

guide.title: Ellipsis and reference
guide.rule: Leave out repeated words only when the intended meaning remains recoverable.
guide.example: Mina chose the blue card and Dara the green one.

guide.title: Emphasis
guide.rule: It-clefts and what-clauses highlight a chosen part of a message. Repeated key terms and clear references help coherence.
guide.example: It was the timetable that changed. What we need is more space.

guide.title: Forms across tenses
guide.rule: A passive uses a form of be and a past participle. The tense belongs to be. Include an agent only when useful.
guide.example: The labels are printed. The labels were being printed.

guide.title: Information and reporting
guide.rule: The passive can keep the same topic across sentences. Reporting passives can use it + passive + that or a subject + passive + infinitive.
guide.example: It is believed that the model is complete. The model is believed to be complete.

guide.title: Services and necessity
guide.rule: Have something done describes arranging a service. Need + -ing can have passive meaning.
guide.example: I had the camera repaired. The lens needs cleaning.

guide.title: Different structures
guide.rule: Conjunctions link clauses; prepositions introduce noun phrases or -ing forms; linking adverbials connect messages across clauses or sentences.
guide.example: Because it rained; because of the rain; it rained, so we stayed.

guide.title: Different relationships
guide.rule: Choose links for addition, cause, result, contrast, alternatives or clarification. Match punctuation to the sentence structure.
guide.example: The room is small. However, it is bright.

guide.title: Signposting
guide.rule: Sequence and summary markers help organise an explanation. Do not use two incompatible links for the same clause connection.
guide.example: Firstly ... secondly ... to sum up.

title: Showing your position in a text

guide.title: Attributing views
guide.rule: Distinguish a personal view, someone else’s claim and an inference.
guide.example: Personally, I prefer the first plan. According to the organiser, it is cheaper.

guide.title: Degree and attitude
guide.rule: Adverbs and adjectives can express certainty, doubt or evaluation. Their position should make the scope clear.
guide.example: It will probably help. It is surprising that attendance fell.

guide.title: Evidence and stance
guide.rule: Verbs such as suggest, believe and argue indicate a writer’s position. Avoid making unsupported generalisations sound certain.
guide.example: The small survey suggests a preference, but does not prove a universal rule.

guide.title: Actions and qualities as nouns
guide.rule: Nominalisation expresses an action or quality as a noun. The form may change, or the same form may serve as noun and verb.
guide.example: Respond → response; clear → clarity; increase → an increase.

guide.title: Describing data
guide.rule: A noun phrase can combine a measured change, its size and its period. Adjective/adverb choice changes with the structure.
guide.example: Attendance rose sharply. There was a sharp rise in attendance.

guide.title: Clarity and responsibility
guide.rule: Nominalisation can make writing compact, but excessive noun chains can hide the agent or meaning. Choose it for a clear purpose.
guide.example: The committee approved the plan. Approval of the plan followed the vote.
